document-model.def: Stores each record as one self-contained document, often JSON, with related data nested inside it. MongoDB is the classic example.

embedding.def: Putting related data inside the document, like an order's items and a copy of its customer, instead of pointing to another table.

data-locality.def: Data that's read together is stored together, so one read fetches it all. The main win of a document.

schema-on-write.def: The database checks every row against a declared structure when it's written. Tables work this way.

schema-on-read.def: Any shape is accepted when written; the code that reads it has to cope with each version. Documents work this way.

graph-model.def: Stores things as nodes and the relationships between them as edges, for data where almost anything can connect to anything.

traversal.def: Following edges from node to node, often to an unknown depth, like friends of friends. SQL does it with a recursive CTE.

lines.hook.1: Maya's bakery lives in tables. Not every system does.
lines.hook.2: Many apps store a whole order as one JSON document. Social apps store who knows whom as a graph.
lines.hook.3: Same data, three shapes. Each makes some questions easy and others painful. Interviewers want to hear which is which.
lines.rel.1: First, the shape you know. To show order one, the database joins four tables: the order, its customer, its items, and their products.
lines.rel.2: Each fact lives once, and joins stitch them back together on every read. That's the relational model.
lines.doc.1: Here's the same order as a document. The customer and the items are nested right inside it.
lines.doc.2: Putting related data inside the document is called <k>embedding</k>. It's the heart of the <k id="document-model">document model</k>.
lines.doc.3: Showing the order is now one read, with no joins. Data that's read together is stored together: <k id="data-locality">data locality</k>.
lines.doc.ask: But Maya's details are copied into her orders. She changes her phone. How many documents must change?
lines.doc.one: If only. Her number is in every one of her orders.
lines.doc.four: Four. One per order she's placed.
lines.doc.sixteen: Not all of them. Just hers: four.
lines.doc.4: It's the update anomaly from the notebook, back again. Documents trade cheap reads for costly updates of copied data.
lines.names.1: Your turn. The documents live in a table called order docs. Pull out each order's ID and the customer's name.
lines.names.ask: Use json extract to reach inside the document.

names.hint.caption: json_extract(doc, '$.customer.name')
names.hint.voice: Json extract, doc, dollar dot customer dot name.

lines.names.error: The database couldn't run that. Check the path: dollar, dot customer, dot name.
lines.names.extra: Too many rows. One per document.
lines.names.missing: Some rows are off. Keep every document, even the walk-ins with no customer.
lines.names.columns: Two columns: the order's ID, and the customer's name.
lines.names.done: Sixteen documents, and the walk-ins come back NULL. The path simply finds nothing.
lines.schema.1: Order eight has a note that no other order has. Nobody declared that field.
lines.schema.2: A table would have refused it: the structure is checked as each row is written. That's <k id="schema-on-write">schema on write</k>.
lines.schema.3: A document accepts any shape. The code that reads it copes with whatever it finds: <k id="schema-on-read">schema on read</k>.
lines.schema.4: Flexible for fields that vary. But every reader now handles every old version, forever.
lines.graph.1: Now the third shape. Some customers brought in friends. Maya brought Ana and Omar, and they brought others.
lines.graph.2: People are nodes, and each referral is an edge between two of them. That's the <k id="graph-model">graph model</k>.
lines.graph.3: Who joined because of Maya, directly or not? Follow the edges one hop at a time until they run out.
lines.graph.4: That's a <k>traversal</k>. Ana and Omar, then Ines and Yuki, then Priya: three hops deep.
lines.graph.5: SQL can do it with a recursive CTE. Graph databases make it the main event, with queries like: follow referred, any depth.
lines.net.1: Your turn. Find everyone Maya brought in, at any depth.
lines.net.ask: Finish the recursive step: join referrals to the people found so far.

net.hint.caption: SELECT r.referred_id FROM referrals r JOIN net ON r.referrer_id = net.id
net.hint.voice: Select the referred I D from referrals, joined to net, where the referrer is someone already in net.

lines.net.error: The database couldn't run that. Check the join inside the CTE.
lines.net.extra: Too many people. Start from Maya's referrals only.
lines.net.missing: Some people are missing. Is the recursive step following the edges from people already found?
lines.net.done: Five people, three hops deep. That's a graph traversal in SQL.
lines.pick.1: So which shape when? Here's how to say it in an interview.
lines.pick.2: Documents when data is read as one tree, like an order or a profile, and rarely joined to much else.
lines.pick.3: Graphs when everything connects to everything, and questions follow links to an unknown depth.
lines.pick.4: Tables for everything in between, which is most things: many-to-many data, reports, and rules to enforce.
lines.pick.ask: A social app shows friends of friends of friends. Which fits most naturally?
lines.pick.graph: Graph. Following links to any depth is exactly what it's built for.
lines.pick.document: A document can hold your own friends list, but friends of friends means following links. That's a graph.
lines.pick.relational: Tables can do it with recursive queries, but it gets slow and awkward at depth. A graph fits more naturally.
lines.pick.5: And the lines blur. PostgreSQL stores JSON columns, and many document databases now do joins. Pick by how the data is read.

quiz.q1.caption: Why is a document store fast at showing a whole order?
quiz.q1.speaker: interviewer

lines.quiz.q1-why: Everything the page needs is embedded in one document, so it's one read with no joins. That's data locality.

quiz.q2.caption: A customer's details are embedded in each of her orders. What goes wrong when she moves?
quiz.q2.speaker: interviewer

lines.quiz.q2-why: Every copy must be updated. Miss one and the documents disagree: the update anomaly again.

quiz.q3.caption: What does schema on read mean?
quiz.q3.speaker: interviewer

lines.quiz.q3-why: Writes accept any shape; the reading code interprets and copes with each variant. Tables check on write instead.

quiz.q4.caption: Which question most needs a graph model?
quiz.q4.speaker: interviewer

lines.quiz.q4-why: Following links to an unknown depth is a traversal: the graph model's strength.

quiz.retry.caption: {right} / 4. Worth another pass.
quiz.retry.voice: Not quite there. Replay a chapter or two, then try again.

lines.finish.1: That's the lesson. Tables store each fact once, documents store what's read together, and graphs store connections. Choose by how the data is read.
